events.goal: Make a verified run mean the acknowledgement reached the enquirer; and until it does, stop the demo and this story describing a check that real runs do not perform.

events.decision_summary: The email half of a verification was not bound to the run. The CRM record is found BY the enquiry's correlation value, so asserting it exists is a real claim; the email event is fetched by message id and the compiler asserted only that its recipient field exists, which proves an email had a recipient, not that it went to the enquirer. A run whose acknowledgement went to the wrong address came back VERIFIED. Meanwhile the demo showed a per-run recipient comparison that no customer workflow performs, and the story documented the plus-tag safeguard of that comparison as if it protected customers. Both surfaces were qualified in the tree today: the demo now composes its rules through the real onboarding compiler and says beside its rule table what the recipient check does not prove; the story labels the plus-tag reasoning as a property of the operator and lists the missing proof under what is not yet true. The fix itself is delivered as a patch proven in an isolated copy, because it touches the frozen contract and another workstream's compiler.
alternatives_considered: Bind at retrieval, mirroring the CRM side. Rejected on the provider's own documentation: Resend retrieves a message by id only, and its list endpoint filters on nothing but a cursor, so no lookup can establish the binding. A connector-side comparison was rejected too: a connector can only report a gap, and a gap is unknown, never failed, while the closure evidence requires FAILED.

A sentinel inside the expected string, avoiding the frozen contract. Rejected: an untyped mini-language inside a string is exactly what the closed rule language exists to prevent, and an empty literal silently changing meaning would upgrade rules that are broken today.
events.decision_reason: Only the evaluator can turn a wrong recipient into CONTRADICTED, and it can only do that if the rule can name a value from the run's own signed event. The proposed change adds one optional field to the assertion contract, expected_from, a closed enum of two names: the event's correlation reference and its expected recipient. Only equals and normalised_email_equals may bind, the literal must be empty when a binding is set, and each binding may address only its counterpart fields. Server code resolves it; nothing is parsed or executed, so the language stays closed, typed and non-executable. A run whose event carries nothing to compare with is UNKNOWN with a new reason code, never a pass. The same binding closes the CRM hole on the record-id locator path, where a record fetched by id can carry a different enquiry's reference.

events.goal: Find out why the billing portal still returned the same URL twice after the fix for exactly that.

events.decision_summary: The page-level fix was right and its case held: a session is minted per click. One layer below, the adapter sent an idempotency key of portal:<customer>:<returnUrl>, which is the same string on every opening for a customer, so Stripe replayed the FIRST session: single-use, short-lived, already spent. That is the expired-session defect reintroduced beneath its own fix, in the one place the existing case could not see because it stubs the gateway. A deterministic key makes a retry safe; a portal opening is not a retry. The key is unique per call now, at the cost of one unused session if a call fails mid-flight, which expires on its own. It was found by running the customer journey against a deployed service rather than by reading the code, which is the only reason it was found at all.

trusting the existing case, rejected: it stubs the gateway and could never reach this line
events.decision_reason: A fix that a lower layer quietly undoes is not a fix.
